note: Hand-written candidate follow-up questions judged by the validator. 'fixture' items reuse the frozen Stage 10F cases (read only, the fixture is untouched); 'holdout' items are NEW answers/domains that no production code or prompt was tuned on. 'good' = a question an interviewer could reasonably ask (a rejection is a FALSE REJECTION); 'bad' = a question that repeats the answer, states the answer, affirms a wrong claim, or targets a covered/other concept (an acceptance is a FALSE ACCEPTANCE). 'known_gap' marks a bad question the rule-based validator cannot detect (it has no technical-truth oracle); the test pins the current behaviour so a change is noticed. These are author judgements, not human validation. Batch 'holdout' (H01-H10) was run once for diagnosis during Stage 10N; batch 'holdout2' (H11-H20) was written BEFORE any validator change and is the untouched confirmation set.

items.question: What is an index in a relational database?
items.answer: An index is a structure that lets the database find rows faster without scanning the whole table.
items.reference: An index speeds lookups but every insert and update must also maintain it, which adds write overhead. Most are B-trees.
good: How would adding several indexes affect a table that receives many inserts?

bad.q: Why does an index find rows faster without scanning the whole table?
What is a B-tree?

items.question: Explain how a hash table works.
items.answer: A hash table maps keys to buckets using a hash function, so lookups are usually constant time.
items.reference: Collisions are resolved by chaining or open addressing; as the load factor grows lookups slow down so tables resize.
good: What happens to lookups when two different keys land in the same bucket?

bad.q: How does the hash function map keys to buckets so lookups are constant time?
Why is a hash table always O(1) in the worst case?
bad.why: false premise handed to the candidate

items.question: What is a Python generator?
items.answer: A generator is a function that uses yield to produce values one at a time instead of building a list.
items.reference: Generators evaluate lazily, keep only the current state in memory and can be iterated only once.
good: What would happen if you tried to loop over the same generator twice?

bad.q: How does a generator use yield to produce values one at a time?

items.question: What is overfitting?
items.answer: Overfitting is when a model does very well on training data but badly on new data.
items.reference: Regularisation, early stopping and more data reduce overfitting, which is detected on a held-out validation set.
good: How would you decide when a model has started to overfit while it is still training?

bad.q: Why does an overfit model do well on training data and badly on new data?

items.question: What does regularisation do?
items.answer: It adds a penalty to the loss so the weights stay small and the model is less likely to overfit.
items.reference: L1 pushes weights to zero and gives sparse models; L2 shrinks them smoothly. Stronger penalties raise bias and lower variance.
good: How would the choice between an L1 and an L2 penalty change the weights you end up with?

bad.q: Why does a penalty on the loss keep the weights small?

items.question: What does a transaction isolation level control?
items.answer: It controls how much one running transaction can see of another one's changes.
items.reference: Stronger isolation prevents dirty and phantom reads but costs concurrency and throughput.
good: What kind of problem could appear if one transaction reads another's uncommitted changes?

bad.q: How much can one running transaction see of another one's changes?

items.question: What is the complexity of merge sort?
items.answer: Merge sort is O(n log n) because it splits the list in half and merges the halves.
items.reference: Merge sort needs O(n) extra memory and is stable, unlike plain quicksort.
good: What does merge sort need that an in-place sort does not?

bad.q: Why is merge sort O(n log n) when it splits the list in half and merges the halves?

items.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
items.answer: A list can be changed after it is created, but a tuple cannot.
items.reference: Tuples are immutable and therefore hashable when their items are, so they can be dictionary keys; lists cannot.
good: Where would you choose a tuple over a list because it cannot change?

bad.q: How is a list changed after it is created while a tuple cannot be?

items.question: What is gradient descent?
items.answer: It updates the weights a little in the direction that reduces the loss, again and again.
items.reference: A learning rate that is too large overshoots and one that is too small is slow; stochastic updates use mini-batches.
good: What would you expect to see if the learning rate were set too high?

bad.q: How does it update the weights in the direction that reduces the loss?

items.question: What is precision?
items.answer: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are really positive.
items.reference: Recall is the share of real positives that were found; raising the threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall.
good: How would moving the decision threshold change precision and what would you give up?

bad.q: What share of predicted positives are really positive?

items.question: What is database normalisation?
items.answer: Normalisation organises tables so the same fact is stored only once.
items.reference: Storing a fact once avoids update anomalies, but joins get costlier so some systems denormalise for read speed.
good: What problem could appear if a customer's address were copied into many rows?

bad.q: Why is the same fact stored only once when tables are organised?

items.question: How does depth-first search work?
items.answer: It goes as deep as it can along one path before backing up and trying the next one.
items.reference: DFS uses a stack or recursion and a visited set so that cycles in a graph do not cause endless loops.
good: What would go wrong if the graph contained a cycle and you kept no record of the nodes you had seen?

bad.q: How does it go as deep as it can along one path before backing up?

items.question: What does the GIL do in CPython?
items.answer: The GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time.
items.reference: CPU-bound code gains nothing from threads under the GIL, so multiprocessing is used, while I/O-bound threads still help because the lock is released while waiting.
good: How would the GIL affect a program that spends most of its time waiting on network calls?

bad.q: Why does the GIL let only one thread run Python bytecode at a time?

items.question: What is cross-validation?
items.answer: You split the data into folds and train several times, each time holding out a different fold.
items.reference: Averaging over folds gives a steadier estimate; preprocessing must be fit inside each fold to avoid leakage, and time series need ordered splits.
good: What could go wrong if you scaled the whole dataset before splitting it into folds?

bad.q: How do you train several times and hold out a different fold each time?

items.question: What is a decision tree?
items.answer: It asks a series of yes or no questions about the features to reach a prediction.
items.reference: Deep trees overfit, pruning limits depth, and splits are chosen by information gain or Gini impurity.
good: What would happen to the tree if you let it keep splitting until every leaf held one example?

bad.q: How does it ask a series of yes or no questions about the features?

items.question: What is a primary key?
items.answer: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.
items.reference: A foreign key in another table refers to a primary key; a composite key uses several columns together when no single one is unique.
good: How would another table refer to a row identified by that key?

bad.q: How does a primary key uniquely identify each row in a table?

items.question: What is dynamic programming?
items.answer: It breaks a problem into smaller overlapping problems and stores their answers.
items.reference: Stored answers are reused through memoisation or tabulation, and the method needs optimal substructure to be correct.
good: What would happen to the running time of a recursive Fibonacci function if you did not store earlier results?

bad.q: How does it break a problem into smaller overlapping problems and store their answers?

items.question: What is a decorator?
items.answer: A decorator is a function that wraps another function to add behaviour.
items.reference: A decorator relies on closures and should use functools.wraps to keep the wrapped function's name; common uses are logging and caching.
good: Where in a real program would you wrap a function this way, and why?

bad.q: How does a function wrap another function to add behaviour?

items.question: What is a confusion matrix?
items.answer: It is a table that counts correct and wrong predictions for each class.
items.reference: The off-diagonal cells are false positives and false negatives, and their costs usually differ, for example in medical screening.
good: Which kind of wrong prediction in the table would worry you more in a medical screening, and why?

bad.q: What does the table count for each class?

items.question: What is k-means?
items.answer: K-means groups points into k clusters by moving centres to the average of their points.
items.reference: The elbow method or silhouette score help choose k, and results depend on the random starting centres.
good: How would you decide how many clusters to use for a dataset you had never seen?

bad.q: How do the centres move to the average of their points?
